newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain mum as Beijing seeks early PLA arrival.
newsitem.headline: Britain mum as Beijing seeks early PLA arrival.

text.p: British officials were tight-lipped on Tuesday about China's late request to march troops into Hong Kong before it officially regains control of the territory on July 1.
Chinese officials meanwhile played down reports of a clash between a Chinese General in charge of an advance party to Hong Kong and Hong Kong customs and immigration officials.
The British silence over the request contrasted with London's forthright rejection of the request earlier this week.

Beijing already has an advance party of about 200 People's Liberation Army (PLA) soldiers in Hong Kong but wants to send more over the border before midnight on June 30 to allow the troops to be in place the minute Chinese rule begins.

Alan Paul, Britain's official at bilateral talks on Tuesday, would not comment on whether the British side had changed its stance that the bulk of the PLA garrison should not set foot in Hong Kong before the Union Jack is lowered for the last time.

"There are still a number of issues relating to the handover, to the transfer of government, which need to be tied up," said Paul, one of London's representatives to the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group (JLG) handling details of Hong Kong's transfer.
Some of the issues were discussed at Tuesday's informal talks, Paul said, but he would not elaborate.
On Monday, China's top official on the JLG said Beijing thought it necessary to deploy more troops before the handover.
"There is a practical need. It is a matter that needs to be resolved and we hope to solve it," Zhao Jihua said.
Zhao's counterpart on the British side, Hugh Davies, gave nothing away after talks on Monday.
"We've made our position clear already," Davies said. "I think the arrival of the PLA will take place around July 1."

Many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people are jittery about the arrival of the PLA, with memories still vivid of Chinese tanks and troops crushing a pro-democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.

Newspaper reports that Major-General Zhou Borong, chief of the PLA advance unit has clashed with Hong Kong officials by insisting on driving through a restricted border area without the necessary permit raised eyebrows.
Zhou later complained that his force had been insulted by colonial authorities, Hong Kong newspapers reported last week.
The South China Morning Post said if the PLA tried to act above the law, they would fail to clean up their "butcher" image.
"This is a storm in a teacup," Chinese JLG representative Chen Zuo'er said.
"Chinese PLA advance party soldiers will obey the laws in Hong Kong, in the past, now and in the future."
In an oblique reference to Hong Kong's concerns, outgoing British Governor Chris Patten said he was certain the PLA would "want to set the best possible example."
"If there are occasional early problems, I'm sure the PLA will want to learn from them and avoid any future difficulties," Patten told reporters.
But Britain and China appear to have achieved some measure of consensus on treaty issues.
The office of Britain's top JLG negotiator said on Tuesday the two sides had reached agreement on how to continue to apply about 200 multilateral treaties to Hong Kong after the handover.

"The mechanism involves the issue of notes to the United Kingdom and the People's Republic of China, complemented by parallel diplomatic notes to be issued to the United Nations Secretary-General by the two governments," the office said in a short statement.
